newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets debt seen calm over U.S. FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets debt seen calm over U.S. FOMC.

text.p: Emerging markets debt remains focused on Tuesday's U.S. monetary policy meeting, but it may not get too excited about either plausible outcome of the session, U.S.-based analysts said.
Like nearly everyone else, emerging debt investors appear perched on the fence, divided over whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates another 25 basis points or leave them unchanged.
Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc, said the market holds a marginal consensus that the Fed will stay its hand this time.
"Without any rate hike, the environment remains stable and positive," Leme said. "But I think it will not be a significant detrimental effect if we were to have such a rate hike."
Goldman's U.S. economists expect another 50 basis points of tightening before yearend, and the market may celebrate only mildly if the Fed keeps rates steady on Tuesday, he said.
"Most likely, it will be neutral to marginally positive for the market," Leme said.
Concerns over U.S. economic growth and inflation would limit the relief, analysts said, as attention shifts to the July 1-2 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
On the flip side, analysts projected at least a limited selloff if central bankers vote a rate hike.
"Should there be an interest-rate hike, it's likely to result in a selloff at least temporarily," said Desmond Lachman, global emerging markets strategist at Salomon Brothers.

While the market would have to come off a bit to accommodate another 25 basis points of U.S. credit tightening, perhaps half the move was priced in already, said Dan Peirce, chief emerging markets strategist at Bank of Boston.
Peirce forecast a credit tightening and mild post-hike selling, but he said a rate shift now would improve the longer-term picture.

"If they tighten, we would definitely view any knee-jerk selloff as a buying opportunity," Peirce said. "But since we view a rate hike as being positive for bonds in the longer term, that would be a short-term effect."
Asked which countries would be most affected by the Fed's decision, Peirce said Ecuador "seems to be in limbo a little bit. They are perhaps a little more reliant on foreign capital."
Argentine debt, which has historically taken much of its direction from Fed policy, may not be so closely linked now, Peirce said.
"I don't think Argentine spreads will really be impacted heavily by (a rate hike)," he said. "You can see it in implied volatilities on FRBs, (which) are very low."

In a Reuters survey, 18 of 39 economists at U.S. primary dealerships forecast a 25-basis-point increase in the key federal funds target rate on Tuesday. Twenty-one of the experts said the Fed would keep fed funds at the current 5.50 percent.
Any change in monetary policy is scheduled to be announced at about 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.
